decisive_factors: B's downside floor is a real cash-flowing business: revenue and EBITDA exist at acquisition close, so even if the AI thesis fails it is an ordinary boutique roll-up with positive value. A has zero revenue until a buyer who has never bought this signs.

B's objections are about price, competition and insurance, which are priced risks and not evidence that no one will buy.

A's pitch contradicts itself and shrinks to a niche. It says control-based pricing but uses a trailing-baseline fee, and the realistic outcome is low single-digit GBP millions at roughly 8-12% EBITDA. About a 30% chance of clearing the first gate multiplies an already small outcome.

B sits in a supply-constrained market with strong tailwinds (restarts, uprates, aging workforce) and active PE demand for these assets, which gives it a credible exit. Its median of about $25M revenue and $30M of value at 7-8x EBITDA is sensible, with real but low odds of the upside.

B is far heavier on capital and founder credentials ($60-75M for the upside, plus a nuclear QA co-founder). Even so, the median case needs only about $8M of enterprise value, largely financed with seller paper, so the expected value per unit of risk is still higher than A's.
result.reasons:
Both ideas were left wounded by their critics, and neither upside is believable. Each critic puts the joint odds at 1-3% or lower. The decision therefore turns on the median outcome and how likely the business is to exist at all.

On that test B is clearly ahead. It buys revenue and EBITDA at close. The pitch holds if the AI hours-saved claim fails, because it then degrades to an ordinary boutique roll-up bought at disciplined multiples with seller notes. B wins on expected outcome and on the probability that a business exists at all.
result.a_biggest_risk: No landlord will buy an outcome-priced carve-out of its worst homes. Buyers are bundling and insourcing, a newco is shut out of procurement, and the signer's reward is small against the legal tail. Behind that sits an unrun premise that the top 5% of homes carry at least 25% of spend and stay persistently expensive.
result.b_biggest_risk: The team cannot buy approved-supplier boutiques at orphan prices (6.5x EBITDA or less) against Arlington, Pelican and New Mountain, and the acquired customers or listing do not survive the ownership change. If so, there is no platform, and every AI or fixed-price claim has nothing to run on.

decisive_factors: Median-case economics: B buys cash-flowing revenue at about 6.5x EBITDA and reaches about $4M EBITDA (about $30M of value) on a small equity cheque. A's own median burns about $28M (plan for $45-60M) and only reaches break-even around year 8-9, on revenue valued at roughly PRGX-style contingent multiples.

Failure mode: if B's AI thesis fails, it is still an ordinary boutique roll-up that owns revenue and EBITDA. If A's realization assumption fails (20% targeted, 5-6% realized), there is no fee base at all.

Core risk is falsifiable and diversified: B's central unknown (hours saved) can be tested in about 13 days for under $10k, and its stop-buying rule caps capital at risk. A's two-week test uses friendly contacts and stated intent, and does not measure whether invoice lines actually fall.

Customer logic: A's 'why pay us' hole is unresolved, since the CFO already owns the capital and Redress/Flexera/in-house sit at parity. B's customers have demonstrable capacity constraints (engineer headcount growth, restarts, uprates) and a real PE bid for these assets (Enercon, Pelican), though that same bid raises acquisition prices.
result.reasons:
Both ideas were wounded by their critics, and both have a thin right tail (A about 2-4% to $100M, B about 1-3% on the critic's math). The difference is in the median and the downside, which carry most of the expected value.

B's median is an acquired $10M-revenue, roughly 15% EBITDA nuclear engineering boutique plus a tuck-in and a small fixed-price lane. That is about $25M revenue and $4M EBITDA, built from real cash flows and a small equity cheque with seller notes and debt. Its tailwinds (restarts, uprates, engineer shortage, PE appetite) are verified. The pitch concedes AI is a cost lever and not a moat, so it does not depend on AI to be a decent business. The main risks are that orphan targets under 6.5x may not exist, that incumbents are capacity-constrained, and that E&O is hard to get. The pitch handles them with bid discipline, a stop rule at month 12, and a fallback to time-and-materials.

A's own author says the median case 'is not a good business'. It burns about $28M to $60M for roughly break-even in year 8-9, and contingent services revenue gets low multiples. The fatal objection is a missing fee base: owners may not release spend, the buyer may not see why it should pay 26-30% for capital it already has, and cheaper advisers sit at parity. B's worst case still leaves a cash-generating asset, while A's worst case leaves a funded engineering team and no fees.
result.a_biggest_risk: Realization: business owners do not release the identified retirable spend, so third-party invoice lines never drop. The only evidence is 20% targeted against 5-6% realized, and the fee base then does not exist. Because the model funds the engineering up front, that outcome means sunk capital with no payback, and the CFO may not pay 26-30% for execution it can do itself or buy from Redress at lower cost.
result.b_biggest_risk: Acquisition supply and price: there may be no approved-supplier nuclear boutiques available at or under 6.5x EBITDA outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes. In that case the thesis cannot start, or it degrades into an overpriced roll-up with no AI productivity edge (hours cut under 15%) and no customer-door advantage.

decisive_factors: Unit economics: B's engineering-services base case earns about 15-20% EBITDA (DP Engineering implied 13-21%). A's only hard cost data (Wisconsin) shows the sector at -12% and the best operator at +2%, with a median case of just 5-8%.

Median-case return: B's median (about $25M revenue, about $4M EBITDA, about $30M value) needs only about $8-15M of acquisition capital. A's median earns $1.3-2M EBITDA on about $25M invested, which its own critic computes as 12-20x EBITDA paid and a capital loss. A's median is effectively a bear case.

Downside floor: B's bear case is still a small, profitable, listed boutique, and AI is a bonus rather than a requirement. A's bear case buys money-losing assets under policy attack, with Medicaid fraud and caregiver crackdowns, DOJ action, and 3504/wage-hour liability like Calderon's $162M.

Testability and demand: B's key unknown (AI hours savings) can be tested in 13 days for under $10k, and it sits on real tailwinds (restarts, uprates, a capacity-constrained incumbent bench). A's key unknown (seller price and cost) has no deal data from any source, the premium-price evidence is cherry-picked, and the near-term RFP window is closed.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are acquisition roll-ups, and both critics rate the upside at roughly 1-3% joint probability, so the choice turns on the median and the floor. On those, B is clearly better.

A buys Medicaid fiscal agents. It admits the competitive-bid price of $68-83 is unprofitable: the Wisconsin FEAs lost 12.5% in aggregate and the best operator made about 2%. The thesis therefore rests on an unproven "premium choice segment" at $150 per participant-month, but real rate cards are $103-121, and Minnesota fees are participant-paid and tiered. The refined plan's median case is $1.3-2M EBITDA on about $25M invested. That implies paying 12-20x EBITDA, which is a capital loss on exit. Revenue is mandated, but it is exposed to state cuts, the federal fraud push, and joint liability for payroll taxes and wage-hour claims. Sponsors (H.I.G., General Atlantic) are already buying the same assets, and no FMS deal price exists. The near-term RFP door (Kentucky) is unenterable.

B buys nuclear engineering boutiques. That is a conventional services roll-up with real margins of 15-20% and a platform buy of about $10M revenue at a defensible 0.7-0.9x revenue (DP Engineering sold at about 0.7x). The median is worth about $30M on modest capital. It has genuine demand tailwinds in restarts and uprates, a thin senior-engineer bench, and capacity-constrained incumbents. Its objections are serious: competition from Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain for targets, E&O coverage for AI work, whether the supplier listing survives an ownership change, and an unproven AI productivity claim. But most are mitigated by structure: liability capped at fees, a stop rule at month 12, and falling back to time-and-materials. If AI fails, it is still an ordinary profitable boutique. A has no equivalent floor.
result.a_biggest_risk: Structural unprofitability. Competitive-bid fees of $68-83 lose money across the sector, and the premium-fee segment that would support margin is unproven. Small operators are therefore either overpriced sponsor targets or loss-making books. At the realistic 5-8% median margin the acquisition math is a capital loss, and the revenue is exposed to state cuts, fraud crackdowns and large employer-liability claims.
result.b_biggest_risk: Sourcing and surviving the acquisition. There may be no supply of listed, non-auctioned boutiques at 6.5x EBITDA or below, because Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain have fresh add-on capital. If so, the thesis reverts to an overpriced consensus roll-up. Acquired customers or QA groups may also react to a re-platformed, AI-assisted workflow, and E&O cover for AI-assisted fixed-price work may be unavailable.

decisive_factors: B's median case is a real cash-flowing acquired business (about $25M revenue, about 17% EBITDA, roughly $4M EBITDA). A's median is about 7% EBITDA on $20M, and the second-round critic's tenure/conversion arithmetic puts it near zero or negative.

A's core mechanic is unproven and probably wrong. A 93% markup ($52 bill on a $27 wage) against a 35-45% staffing norm, when shops can hire direct at $24-28 and train. Both A critics rated competition and customer objections fatal, while B's three critics rated theirs serious.

B's demand tailwind is real: restarts, uprates, a thin engineer pipeline, and incumbents hiring about 15% a year and capacity-constrained. Buying an existing book also starts revenue at close, with no greenfield sales cycle or 6-18 month alliance cycles.
B degrades gracefully. If the AI productivity result fails it becomes an ordinary boutique roll-up with a tolerable return. A has no fallback: below roughly $47.50 an hour the business is dead.

Tail odds are similar (both about 1-3% for $100M+), so the median and floor decide it. The upside-case dependence on $60-75M of capital and multiple arbitrage is B's main drag, but the median needs only about $10M.
result.reasons:
Both tails are long shots, and both second-round critics put the $100M outcome at about 1-3%, so the decision rests on the median outcome and the floor. B's median is an acquired $10M-revenue nuclear boutique plus a tuck-in, roughly $25M revenue and about $4M EBITDA. At 7-8x that is worth about $30M. It is bought with seller notes at modest equity, in a sector with real tailwinds (restarts, uprates, aging workforce, incumbents capacity-constrained). Revenue starts at close. If the AI productivity thesis fails, it is still an ordinary roll-up with customers and a listed QA program.

A has no comparable floor. Its median is about $20M at 7% EBITDA, and the second-round critic's arithmetic puts it near zero. Tenure and conversion contradict each other. WIOA subsidies likely do not apply to hired-out staffing. The 93% markup runs against a 35-45% norm, and shops can hire directly at $24-28 and train. Both of A's first-round critics called the competition and customer objections fatal, and it has no moat. Staffing margins and multiples are low, and wage inflation breaks break-even at roughly $47.50 an hour.

B's risks (sourcing at orphan prices against Pelican and Arlington, the credentialed co-founder gate, E&O insurability) are serious but more recoverable. Insurance can fall back to time-and-materials, and the bid cap stops overpaying.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops and fleets will not pay a staffing-style bill rate of $50+ an hour (a 93% markup) for 6-week trainees when they can hire direct at $24-28 and train. Below about $47.50 an hour the business loses money, and conversion terms and wage inflation erode the margin further.
result.b_biggest_risk: Failing to buy credible ASL-listed nuclear boutiques at or below about 6.5x EBITDA against Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain, which would leave an ordinary roll-up with no AI cost edge. This is compounded by the need for a credentialed nuclear QA co-founder and by the risk that customers or the supplier listing do not survive the change of ownership.

decisive_factors: Floor and fatality: B's median case is an ordinary cash-flowing nuclear engineering boutique bought at a disciplined price, with revenue and customers from day one. Its killer assumption (AI cuts hours 30%+) only affects the upside. A's killer assumption (an unaffiliated plan pays a fixed fee) is unevidenced and decides every case, including the median.

Value per dollar of revenue: B's median is about $25M revenue at ~17% EBITDA (~$4M EBITDA, ~$30M value), and its upside would run 20%+ margins. A's $100M upside is only ~$14M EBITDA at ~34% gross margin, and the 'median' is conditional on surviving a test with no demand evidence (the critic says 55-60% odds of under $5M).

Demand and buyer health: B sells to nuclear owners who are credit-worthy, supply-constrained and in a secular build-out (restarts, uprates, engineer shortage), and revenue is bought rather than won. A sells to Medicaid plans that are shrinking, cutting SG&A and insourcing or buying from CareBridge, with 12-30 month cycles and thin labor margins (R3 priced at 95% of in-house cost yet targeting a 10-15% margin).

Capital at risk: A's seed money buys 12-18 months of selling with no revenue anchor and nothing to resell if the pitch fails. B's first dollars buy an earning asset with seller-note and earn-out protection, a stop-buying rule at month 12, and a bake-off test under $10k.

Both survive only as 'wounded', but B's weaknesses (a crowded PE trade, price discipline, E&O, hiring) are execution and price risks on a real business. A's weaknesses are existential: no moat, no revealed demand, and a dossier that explicitly says not to pursue it as a standalone company.
result.reasons:
B is the better expected outcome, mainly because its failure modes are about price and returns while A's are about whether a business exists at all.

B's median case is a bought, cash-generating nuclear engineering boutique. It has existing approved-supplier status and customers, and it sells into a durable, supply-constrained market with a labor shortage. Its core unproven claim, that AI cuts total hours by 30% or more, is what separates the upside from a plain roll-up, but the base case does not need it. That claim can be tested for under $10k in about two weeks. The weaknesses are real: the consensus Pelican/Arlington trade, thin evidence for orphan-priced supply, E&O insurability, key-person dependence on a nuclear QA co-founder, and an upside that is mostly bought revenue. But they mostly compress returns rather than zero them. Even a 1-3% shot at the upside sits on top of a roughly $4M EBITDA median.

A has real operational pain (missed shifts, ratio-bound coordination) and a cheap test, but the existential question stays open: whether a non-Elevance, non-UHC plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee. Rival plans already buy from CareBridge, and large plans insource. The remaining buyers are sub-scale plans with the thinnest budgets, in a shrinking Medicaid market, with long cycles and a state sign-off for each deal. The dollars-per-revenue picture is poor. The $100M case is about $14M EBITDA, and the key labor rung has an unexplained margin gap. The dossier itself says not to pursue it as a standalone company.

On probability times payoff, B has a materially better floor and a comparable or better payoff.
result.a_biggest_risk: No demand: no non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan may pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans may insource, buy from CareBridge or the Carelon family, or insist on savings-only. The labor rung's thin margin (a 10-15% target at 95% of in-house cost) is a second structural weakness.
result.b_biggest_risk: Acquisition economics. Enough approved-supplier nuclear boutiques may not be available at or below about 6.5x EBITDA, since Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain have add-on mandates and capital. If so, the roll-up either stalls or is bought at 9-12x, and the AI productivity edge is unproven, so the result collapses to an ordinary low-return boutique.

decisive_factors: Floor and median: B buys cash-flowing, already-listed boutiques, so its median (about $25M revenue, about $4M EBITDA, roughly $30M of value) is a real profitable company. A's median ($30M revenue, 11-13% gross margin, about $4-5M gross profit) is roughly break-even after a 25-person team.

Fatality of objections: A's three critiques were all rated fatal, and its own dossier calls it dead as a startup. The gap it claims (nobody holds stock) is false, and the supply side (OEM slot assignability, cancelled units) is unevidenced. B's objections were rated serious, and its fallback (an ordinary boutique roll-up if AI productivity fails) still works.

Durability of demand: B sells into growing, structurally supply-constrained demand (restarts, uprates, engineer headcount rising from about 7k to about 10k). A depends on a shortage premium that Rystad says has stalled and that new OEM capacity in 2027-29 erodes, as A's own pre-mortem concedes.

Upside quality: B's upside has a real margin lever (AI cutting hours, 20%+ EBITDA), though only a 1-3% shot. A's upside is capped by a dealer spread of about $8-12M EBITDA, also a 2-3% shot, with no moat.

Capital and downside: A's early deals hold unit and price-mark-down risk on a commodity with no pricing power. B's capital goes into going-concern assets, bid-capped at 6.5x with a stop rule at month 12, so a miss is a smaller loss.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither upside is likely (about 1-3% each after the second-round critics). The choice turns on the floor, the median and which objections kill the idea.

A is a dealer-financier in a market where JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon, Ayr and FluxCo already sell fast or stocked units. Its premise of premium pricing for date-certain delivery is unproven. Its supply plan (OEM slot access for a newcomer, assignable cancelled units) has no evidence and is not covered by its own two-week test. Its margin is an 8-13% spread with no moat at launch. Its window is closing as OEM capacity lands in 2027-29. The refined pitch's most likely outcome is failing its own test. If it passes, the median is roughly break-even.

B has real weaknesses: the AI productivity claim is unmeasured on calculation-grade work, it needs a nuclear QA insider, E&O insurance is uncertain, the customer doors (the buyer co-op, primes, thin-bench owners) are unproven, and orphan-price evidence rests on two data points from one failed roll-up. But it buys existing revenue and EBITDA, so it does not depend on winning new customers from entrenched alliances. Its pricing math is internally consistent. Demand is growing and constrained. Even with no AI edge it is a boutique roll-up worth about $30M, and the 13-day, under-$10k bake-off tests the right unknown. The expected value is higher for B, and its failure modes are less likely to wipe out the whole investment.
result.a_biggest_risk: The core gap does not exist: incumbent dealers already deliver warranted units fast, and no OEM will give a newcomer slots or accept unit transfers. Without that supply the business is a thin-spread broker with no pricing power and no moat, in a shortage that new capacity erodes from 2027.
result.b_biggest_risk: Acquisition economics and execution. Orphan ASL-listed boutiques may not be buyable at 6.5x EBITDA or less against Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain, and the AI procedure layer may not hold up (productivity under 15%, customers leaving after the ownership change, or no affordable E&O). Any of these leaves an ordinary low-margin staffing-like roll-up.

decisive_factors: B's median case is a real, cash-flowing business bought on day one (about $25M revenue, roughly $4M EBITDA, about $30M of value). A's median is about $7-12M revenue at breakeven EBITDA, with a 45% chance of not signing a second client.

A's value proposition is unproven and probably wrong. The operator must run 17-24% cheaper than the hospital's own cost, using an unbenchmarked 15-18% baseline and with no route density. It sells a 5-year contract to health-system CFOs who can do the work in-house or take a national's offer, and no precedent of a non-national operator renewing was found.

A's upside is mostly pass-through revenue at about 8% EBITDA with sponsor-owned JV economics. That makes the $110M case worth far less to founders than its revenue suggests. B's upside has roughly 20%+ margins, but about $65M of it is bought, so it leans on deal supply and price.
A had three critiques rated fatal, and the second-round critic put its upside at 1-3%. B's three were rated serious, and its failure mode is a plain boutique roll-up, not zero.

The remaining risk in B is mainly financial. It needs $60-75M of capital and a nuclear QA/licensing co-founder for the upside, but the median needs far less and the stop rule at month 12 limits the loss. A's risk is demand that may not exist.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and both quote an upside probability of about 1-5%. The better business is the one whose median and downside cases are worth more, because that is where most of the probability sits.

B buys existing, profitable, approved-supplier nuclear engineering boutiques under a hard bid cap (6.5x EBITDA, 30% seller note or earn-out) and a stop rule. Even if the AI thesis fails, it is an ordinary boutique roll-up with real EBITDA. Nuclear engineering is capacity-constrained: operating-plant engineer demand rises from about 7,000 FTE to 9,000-10,000 by 2030. Strategic and PE buyers (Pelican, Arlington, New Mountain) pay for these assets, so the exit is credible. The test is a roughly $10k bake-off on the one load-bearing unknown.

A is a different kind of bet. The rebuild fixed the legal structure (100% hospital-owned LLC, cost-plus, no percentage fees), but the cost it charges is below what the buyer pays itself only if a startup out-operates the hospital by about 20%. The input numbers are admitted guesses, and no benchmark exists. The buyer is a health-system CFO who can insource, buy cheap advice from Mayo, ARUP or Chi, or take a national's management offer. The one documented customer of this model (Kootenai) fired its operator. At A's median, the company is breakeven. At its upside, revenue is mostly pass-through, so $110M of revenue is worth perhaps $80-130M.

A's test is cheaper ($2k versus $10k), but a cheap test of a weak thesis does not make it a better business. B wins on expected value.
result.a_biggest_risk: No non-selling health system signs a 5-year open-book contract with a startup at a price at least 8% below its own cost. The cost advantage rests on an unbenchmarked 15-18% baseline and no route density. The buyer's alternatives (in-house, Mayo/ARUP/Chi advice, a national's management offer) are all cheaper to accept, and a successful operator tends to be bought by a national, as PAML was.
result.b_biggest_risk: The buy side. There may be no ASL-listed boutiques at or below 6.5x EBITDA outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes. Customers and supplier status must also survive the change of control. If the team has to pay 9-12x, or customers leave after the AI procedure is added, the business becomes an overpriced staff-augmentation roll-up with an unproven AI edge. The 30% hours-saved assumption is the second gate.

decisive_factors: Capital at risk versus return: A needs $130-175M of outside equity and $340M of uses for roughly 1.8-3.3x gross even in its own upside case, and the conditional median is about 1x. B's median case needs about $10-15M of equity and its upside needs $30-40M.

Failure mode and floor: A's unconditional median is $0, with about a 35% chance of even closing a first deal. B buys cash-flowing revenue at a hard price cap, so the bear case is a small roll-up at roughly cost, and a stop rule limits the loss. B's critics rated it serious, not fatal.

Keystone behavior: A depends on an OEM prepaying a non-incumbent owner, which three critics and the researcher found no precedent for. A also has no customer-side reason to route the money through a new owner rather than sign directly with the plant's current owner. B's median case works without any novel customer behavior.

Cost and speed of the test: B's riskiest assumption (AI cuts hours by 30% or more) can be tested in 13 days for under $10k. B also gets revenue at acquisition close. A's capacity lands in 2028-29 and its test depends on cold access to OEM procurement leads.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and both are buy-and-build plays. I scored them on probability times value against the capital each needs.

A is a capital-allocation bet. A first-time sponsor must raise $130-175M of equity, win a qualified superalloy caster against GE/CPP, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters, and then persuade OEMs to prepay at a non-incumbent owner. Nobody has found a precedent for that prepayment. All three critics called it fatal, and the refined pitch's own odds are about 12% with an operator and an equity partner already in hand. The structural gap was never answered: if customers fund the line anyway, they can sign with the current owner directly. Even the upside case returns only about 1.8-3.3x gross, and it depends on a turbine order cycle that peaks around 2026-2030. The median case, a $45M plant bought at about 2x revenue, earns little over its cost.

B is a more ordinary business, and that is a strength. Its median case is a $25M-revenue boutique at 15-17% EBITDA, bought at a capped price for roughly $10-15M of equity. That is a respectable outcome with a floor. Its AI edge is unproven, and the owner value proposition is thin. But the critics rated it serious, not fatal, and it does not need the AI edge to produce the median. It has limited downside because it stops buying if nothing clears the cap. Revenue starts at the first closing, the demand backdrop of restarts, uprates and an engineer shortage is real, and the key unknown can be tested for under $10k in about two weeks. Its $110M upside is probably only 1-3% likely, but it does not carry the outcome.

B wins by a clear margin on expected outcome, with lower capital and a better chance of being worth something.
result.a_biggest_risk: The keystone customer behavior has no precedent: a non-captive OEM signing a multi-year, dollar-denominated reservation with make-whole to fund a line at a non-incumbent-owned caster. Without it the capital stack does not close, and customers have little reason to route that money through a new owner when they can sign with the current owner directly. Buying a qualified asset at a sane price against GE/CPP, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters is a close second.
result.b_biggest_risk: There may be no supply of quality, approved-supplier-listed nuclear boutiques at 6.5x EBITDA or less outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes. The business would then buy nothing, or overpay for a commodity roll-up, while its one differentiator, a 30% or greater AI hours cut with independent verification, stays unproven. The ASL listing and customers may also not survive the change of ownership.

decisive_factors: Value if it works: B's upside is roughly $110M revenue at 20%+ EBITDA (about $22M) in a sector with 9-12x specialist multiples. A's $108M revenue is only about EUR 6M EBIT and is explicitly hold-forever with no exit.
Even the median case favors B. About $25M revenue at about 17% EBITDA is about $4M and sellable. A's median is about EUR 0.8M group EBIT (about 3.5%), a small regional service group.

A's core economics are invented and reverse-fitted (the 19% contribution and EUR 240k overhead). Its own marginal-economics logic says any neighbouring firm absorbs a closing owner's book more cheaply than a new hub. Adverse selection means the books on offer are the worst ones.
A's capital structure is internally contradictory. It needs EUR 28-30M of no-exit equity at a capped 6-8% yield from LPs who are not identified, using a legal wrapper that has not been tested.

B has a floor even if its AI thesis fails: a bid-disciplined boutique roll-up that stops buying at its price cap. B's key productivity risk can be killed in 13 days for under $10k, and the margin math (break-even price cut = 0.65 x hours cut) is sound. Probabilities are similar (both about 1-5%), so the larger payoff and better downside decide it.
result.reasons:
I weighed expected outcome across three things: payoff if it works, probability, and capital/time. The probabilities are comparable. A's own estimate is 3-5% and its critic says 1-2%. B's own estimate is 5-8% and its critic says 1-3%. Both second-round critics rated their idea wounded. So the payoff and the floor decide it.

B wins on payoff. A $110M-revenue nuclear engineering house at 20%+ EBITDA is a $150M+ enterprise. A $108M-revenue Handwerk network earns about EUR 6M EBIT and is built never to be sold, so it has no exit. A's margins are structurally thin, at 3.5% group EBIT in the median case. That is a founder-carry business, not a value-creation story.

B's median case is also better. It is an ordinary boutique roll-up with about $4M of EBITDA at 13-21% margins. That is sellable to Pelican, Arlington or New Mountain, all of whom have add-on mandates. A has no such buyer.

A's central model is fragile. The 19% contribution and EUR 240k overhead are invented, and the model is fitted so that a hub breaks even. If extra revenue is nearly free for a firm with spare capacity, incumbents and neighbours beat a new hub on price. Sellers who cannot sell are also the ones with the weakest books. The capital ask is the likeliest cause of death: no-exit equity at a capped yield, from LPs who have not been identified.

B's weaknesses are real but bounded. Incumbents are entrenched, insurance for AI-produced work is uncertain, and no acquisition may clear the 6.5x cap. But it has a stop rule, so it simply buys less, and the productivity claim can be tested in 13 days for under $10k.
result.a_biggest_risk: The economics of the absorbed books are unproven and adverse-selected: owners who cannot sell hold the weakest, most consumer-heavy books, and the 19% contribution and 70% retention are invented. Combined with an unfinanceable no-exit capital structure, this likely leaves a sub-EUR 1M EBIT regional group at best.
result.b_biggest_risk: Acquisition supply at the price cap. If no quality approved-supplier boutique is available at or below 6.5x EBITDA outside the Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain processes, there is no platform. The unproven AI hours cut also leaves nothing to differentiate it from those better-funded roll-ups.

decisive_factors: B's median case is a profitable business (about $25M revenue, roughly 17% EBITDA, about $4M EBITDA, worth about $30M), while A's median is break-even to a small loss on about $30M of mostly pass-through revenue.

A's economics are thin and may be negative: the claimed 10-12% gross margin falls to about 3-4% once the ISP-price alternative, bond premiums, bid costs, liquidated damages and site management are counted. Passing A's own demand gate (10%+ scope growth) selects for the outages where the prime loses money.

Downside shape: B buys existing cash flow and caps liability at fees, so failure degrades to an ordinary boutique roll-up. A takes uncapped fixed-price scope-growth and schedule risk, needs $40-60M of risk capital, a surety line and a sponsor, and has no hardware, references or moat for 4+ years.
Upside payoff per unit of probability: B's $110M revenue at 20%+ margin is about $20M+ EBITDA, even at 2-8% odds. A's $110M upside is only $4-7M EBITDA at about 3% odds.

Objection severity: A drew three fatal critiques (Hanwha can copy it, buyers score references and bonds, the insurer wrap is probably uninsurable). Its refinement removed the wrap and left demand, supply slots and the sponsor unproven. B's critiques were rated serious and are mostly about entry route, price and execution, and the refinement removed the QA-moat and developer-line dependencies.

Tailwinds and time to revenue: B has tight nuclear-engineering labor, restarts and uprates, and revenue from the day the first acquisition closes. A's first revenue is spring 2028 at the earliest, behind six gates.
result.reasons:
B wins on expected outcome. Both ideas are wounded, but their failure modes differ.

A is a risk-bearing middleman. It sells fixed-price, date-guaranteed, bonded outages with no owned hardware, no references and no insurer backstop. Its gross margin is already thin at about 12%, and a prime paying shops roughly 0.87x of the OEM price nets only 3-4% before bonds, bid costs and liquidated damages. Its own pass test (owners facing 10%+ scope growth) selects the jobs where it loses money. Rotor and casting slots sit with the competitors it would depend on. Hanwha can match the cap within 18-24 months. Even the upside is only $4-7M EBITDA at about 3% probability. The median is a subscale business that breaks even or loses money, with real balance-sheet tail risk.

B is mostly a conventional niche roll-up with an AI cost lever added. It buys EBITDA-positive, already-qualified nuclear engineering boutiques, caps liability at fees per deliverable, and gets revenue from acquisition close. Even if AI delivers nothing, it is an ordinary boutique roll-up in a sector with tight labor, restarts, uprates and heavy PE interest. That roll-up is worth roughly $30M at the median, and the critics put the bear case at stalling under $15M, not at zero. The upside is a large EBITDA outcome (about $20M+), so even 2-8% odds carry far more value than A's. B's weak points are real. The orphan-price supply is thinly evidenced, the AI productivity claim is untested, and the upside is mostly bought revenue. These are risks to the size of the win, whereas A's risks go to whether it has a product and a margin.

B needs a credentialed nuclear QA co-founder and meaningful capital. That is a real hurdle, but it is within what a capable team can do.
result.a_biggest_risk: Unit economics and adverse selection. Real margin is roughly 3-4% rather than 12%, because owners with the most scope growth are the only ones who value the cap, and those are the jobs where the prime loses money. The prime carries uncapped fixed-price tail risk with no hardware, references, sponsor or surety line, and ISPs control the scarce rotor and casting slots.
result.b_biggest_risk: Acquisition sourcing and price. A first-time team must find and close ASL-listed 30-100 person boutiques at 6.5x EBITDA or less while Pelican, Arlington and New Mountain (all with fresh capital) are buying. The cheap targets are probably low-margin staff-augmentation shops, and customers or listings may not survive the change of control. If this fails, the business never reaches scale. The related fallback risk is that AI cuts under 15% of hours, which leaves only an ordinary roll-up.

decisive_factors: Intermediaries in A's market have reached $100M+ with tens of millions of capital in the same shortage (Ayr over $500M orders on $25M raised, Giga over $150M infrastructure sales, JCL, Maddox). No neutral operator in B's market has an equivalent existence proof.
A needs about $30M equity and has a bounded matched-book structure. B needs $50-80M, 12-18 months to a first paid pilot, and 24 months of runway against 18-30 month plan sales cycles.

A's demand pain is documented and acute: 128-160+ week lead times, with buyers already paying 3-15% premiums and prepaying for slots. B's demand is unevidenced. Its R1 pain (exception rates) is unmeasured, its R3 cost advantage is asserted, and its price exceeds in-house cost for larger plans.

B's buyers are in distress (Elevance, Centene, Molina and Aetna shrinking or exiting markets) and its largest potential buyers insource. The margin squeeze B uses as a tailwind is the same squeeze that cuts vendor budgets. A's buyers are utilities and EPCs/IPPs with funded projects.

B has the higher value if it works (recurring revenue, about $14M EBITDA on $101M), but its upside probability is only 1-2% by the critic's estimate, and its R3 labor rung is structurally thin-margin. A's upside is lower quality (transactional, cyclical, about $8-12M EBITDA on $120M) but faster and cheaper to reach. The result is close.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and neither is a venture-grade margin pool. I picked A narrowly on probability, capital and speed, not on the size of the upside.

A's economics are poor: 5-10% blended gross margin, no moat at launch, incumbents who already sell stocked units, and a shortage premium that new OEM capacity should compress in 2027-29. Its supply side (OEM slots or assignable cancelled units for a newcomer) is also unevidenced and sits outside the two-week test. B has the better asset if it works, since recurring contracts valued like Evolent or CareCentrix would be worth more than a dealer spread. But B's path to that asset is longer and less probable.

The base rates differ. Intermediaries in transformers have scaled quickly on small capital during this shortage, and the demand signal is concrete. A capable team can reach matched-book sales within 3-12 months, with downside capped by the guardrails (title only on a PO or a 12%+ discount, 6-month hold cap). Even if the premium compresses, the fallback is a profitable small dealer-broker. The median case is thin (about $30M revenue, near break-even to a few million of EBITDA), but it is real revenue on modest equity.

B asks a cold entrant to sell fixed-fee Medicaid operations to plans that are cutting administrative costs, insourcing, or already buying from CareBridge. Its neutrality pitch was dropped. The remaining claim is a 15-20% cost advantage in a ratio-bound labor business. The scale argument only works for sub-scale plans, which have the smallest budgets. Capital need is higher and the first paid pilot is 12-18 months out.

On probability times value, A's lower probability of a large outcome is offset by lower capital, a faster feedback loop and a more usable fallback. B has the better asset if it works, but a lower chance of getting there.
result.a_biggest_risk: Supply access and a closing window. Allied OEMs may not give a newcomer slots or transfer cancelled units, and dealers already sell stocked or fast units. If new capacity lands in 2027-29, the date-certain premium falls toward a 5% dealer spread, leaving a thin-margin, capital-heavy broker with no moat.
result.b_biggest_risk: No evidence that a non-Elevance plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Shrinking, cost-cutting plans insource or buy from CareBridge. Even if they buy, R3 (licensed coordination, where the $100M case lives) needs a 10-15% margin at 95% of the plan's in-house cost in a caseload-ratio-bound labor business, so the company may stall at R1-R2 (about $55-60M cap) or at boutique scale.

decisive_factors: Buyer behaviour: A's first-round critics rated customer demand and execution/procurement 'fatal', and the evidence points the wrong way (landlords bundle whole-stock deals and insource; no carve-out precedent found). All three of B's first-round objections were 'serious', not fatal, and plans do already buy outsourced HCBS operations and coordination.

Product shape: B sells substitution for budget lines plans already carry (admin and care-coordination) with no risk licence and little capital in R1-R2. A's first rungs depend on a post-hoc concentration claim (top 5% of homes carrying 25% or more of spend, persistent) that nobody has measured, then on a full winter of randomised-control evidence before the real product can be sold.

Structural access: A's newco is shut out of the procurement door (turnover and D&B tests, exclusivity inside incumbents' scope), so the realistic end state is a subcontractor to Mears or Wates at prime margins of about 5%. B has a plausible regional or second-source entry in the plans too small to build a 24/7 desk, and a path to $55-60M even without R3.

Market size and exits: B's pool is about $1.2-1.8B a year in plan spend, and it has live comparables (CareBridge, Cityblock, Evolent, CareCentrix, HHAX) plus a buyer universe for an exit. A is a UK-only niche worth about GBP570-620M of existing spend, 20% of which is pass-through works at 8-12% EBITDA, with a credible residual of low single-digit GBP millions.

Internal contradictions: A's pricing contradicts its own headline (the capitated rung uses a trailing baseline with an index, and no concurrent control can exist there), and randomised waitlists collide with Awaab's Law. B's weak points (R3 margin asserted, 'neutral' dropped as the reason to buy) are real but bounded, and the R1-R2 test is cheap and decisive.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are weak as $100M businesses, and both of their own dossiers say so. The question is which has the higher probability-weighted outcome for a capable team, and I think that is B.

A's objections look closer to fatal. The customer critic found no evidence anyone buys a cohort carve-out, and landlords are bundling (Livin, Thurrock, Winchester) or insourcing (Teign, Basildon). The execution critic found a newco cannot clear turnover and D&B gates, and the scope sits inside incumbents' exclusive contracts. The realistic route is subcontracting to Mears or Wates at about 5% margins, and Wates already sells Healthy Homes. The product's value also depends on an unmeasured concentration premise and a causal effect that takes about 20 months and a winter to prove. Its pricing is internally inconsistent, and a randomised control collides with Awaab's Law. The second-round critic's honest residual is low single-digit GBP millions at 8-12% blended EBITDA.

B has a real, large, existing spend pool and a buyer type that routinely outsources admin and coordination. Its first rungs are fixed-fee substitutions, so the sale is a cost comparison rather than category creation. The sub-scale plans (5-60k HCBS members) are plausible customers, since a 24/7 desk has a staffing floor. B's fatal-looking risks are bounded and testable in two weeks for about $3k. The $100M case is 1-2% likely, but a competent execution plausibly reaches an $18M-revenue regional services business, and a strategic exit is available. B's weaknesses are that it needs $50-80M of capital if it scales, R3 is a thin-margin labour business, and demand for non-Elevance fixed fees is unproven. Even so, these look less likely to be fatal than A's structural exclusion from the buyer.
result.a_biggest_risk: No buyer and no door: landlords are bundling disrepair work into whole-stock partner contracts or insourcing, no carve-out precedent exists, and a newco cannot clear the turnover and D&B tests. The business collapses into a low-margin subcontractor to Mears or Wates, or the unmeasured hot-spot concentration and persistence premise fails.
result.b_biggest_risk: Non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plans will not pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. They insource (Centene has 338K lives in-house), buy from CareBridge as Iowa's plans did, or insist on savings-only. Behind that, R3 coordination capacity may not be profitable at 95% of in-house cost, because caseload ratios stop automation from cutting headcount.

decisive_factors: B has a cheap, decisive test of a real edge (a 13-day, under-$10k bake-off on AI-assisted hours). A has no proprietary edge to test, only an untested guess that sellers will pick it

A's returns are mostly entry-price discipline plus multiple expansion (about 6.5x to 9.5x). Its own median is about 8% IRR and its upside is about 3.5x, so even a win is capped. B sits in a growing, talent-constrained niche with higher exit multiples

Capital and founder economics favor B. Its median needs about $8M EV and low-seven-figure setup money, against A's $45M+ of acquired revenue and a sponsor take of fees plus thin carry. B's founders own an operating company

B's fatal risks (AI productivity, insurance) surface early and cheaply, and its floor is a decent niche boutique. A's fatal risk (strategics and PE out-bid it) is structural, and a win only yields a mediocre, undifferentiated roll-up
result.reasons: Both ideas are wounded, and I put B ahead only narrowly. A is a conventional buy-and-build of family uniform laundries. Its own refined pitch scores it 4/10, with a median of about 8% IRR and an upside of about 3.5x that depends on the exit multiple expanding. At least ten funded buyers and four strategics chase the same targets. Strategic prints of 2.3-3.3x revenue anchor sellers far above the 0.85-1.0x revenue offer. Rollover plus a family role is already the PE default (Falcon, A&M, Calera). Any seller who accepts probably has a reason other than the offer. A wins only if it can buy at or below 6.5x, and it has nothing structural to make that happen. It also needs three times B's capital to reach a similar absolute outcome. The sponsor's take at the median is small: a closing fee, a management fee and little carry. B is also a consensus roll-up, and its upside is 1-3% likely by the critic's count, so a long shot. Its edge is thin, its supplier doors are mostly locked by alliances, and Pelican has the same thesis. But the one thing that could separate B from a plain roll-up, AI-driven hours savings, can be tested in two weeks for under $10k. Its median needs little capital, and the end market grows (engineering headcount up about 35% by 2030, with talent scarce and PE paying 9-12x). Its floor is a decent niche boutique, and it stops buying rather than overpaying. The risks of A are structural and untestable until money is spent, and the risks of B can be killed cheaply.
result.a_biggest_risk: Sellers will not accept 5.5-6.5x with rollover when Alsco, Wildman or a PE platform offers about 8x or more in cash. Without an edge, any deal the team wins is adversely selected, and returns fall to about 4-12% IRR.
result.b_biggest_risk: The AI productivity claim fails on real calculation-grade work (hours cut under 15-30% with 90%+ first-pass acceptance). Then there is no price edge and the business is a worse version of Pelican's nuclear roll-up. Orphan targets, uninsurable fixed-price risk and entrenched alliances compound it.

decisive_factors: Buyer breadth and diversification: A sells to roughly 700 reachable US companies through CFO/PE/M&A triggers, while B sells to 6-10 non-Elevance, non-UHC parents plus 15-25 unsized regional plans, each with a veto and 12-30 month cycles. That is the Evolent concentration failure mode.

Offer asymmetry: A's offer is 'no invoice line drops, no fee', with a paid X-ray credited against the fee, so the buyer takes no downside. B asks a plan to take on delegation oversight, state sign-off and transition risk for about 5% savings (95% of in-house cost). B's margin claim (10-15% at that price in a ratio-bound labor business) is asserted, not derived.

Evidence of demand and why-now: B has no sign any plan will pay a fixed fee, and the market's revealed behavior is insourcing or buying CareBridge. B's buyers are shrinking: Elevance, Centene and Aetna are exiting states, MLRs are rising and H.R.1 cuts begin in 2028. A has a documented real pain (CFOs funding AI spend, M&A synergy targets, sponsor exits, platform end-of-support) and metered precedent in PRGX and recovery audit. A's risk is follow-through, not whether the buyer exists.

Cost of being wrong and profit shape of the tail: A is gated, can be tested for about $0 in 14 days, and has a boutique fallback with paid X-rays. B needs $50-80M and 12-18 months to a first paid pilot. If A's upside lands, it carries roughly 50% contribution margin (about $30M+ EBITDA on $100M revenue). B's upside is about $14M EBITDA on $100M, and a critic puts it at 1-2% odds.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded, and both authors and critics put the $100M case at low single-digit odds. The median outcome of each is a thin-margin services company, so the choice comes down to which has the cheaper, faster path to a real business and the less fatal objections.

A's core objection is realization. Owners released only 5-6% against a 20% target in the one panel found, and the 'why pay us' answer is roughly parity with doing it in-house. That is serious, but it is also the one assumption the idea tests first, cheaply. The fee is metered by third-party invoices, and the buyer risks nothing if no line drops. The buyer set is wide and spans industries, with a CFO signer and event-driven urgency. There is no licensing or delegation friction. If realization is near 25%, A dies cleanly and early, losing little capital. If realization is above 50%, it works at a boutique scale of $10-20M before any venture-scale question arises.

B's objections are closer to fatal. No plan has asked for a non-Elevance vendor, rivals already buy from CareBridge or insource, and the author drops the neutrality thesis, so no differentiated reason to buy remains. The offer is a fixed price at 95% of the plan's in-house cost for work that is ratio-bound and labor-heavy. The buyer cohort is small, volatile and shrinking in late 2026. Revenue arrives only after 12-30 month cycles. The $100M case needs the thin-margin R3 rung, and even then it yields about $14M of EBITDA. The author's own odds are 55-60% for under $5M revenue.

A's weaknesses are a revenue cliff after the 36-month tail, valuation at about 1x contingent revenue, and capital needs of $28-60M. They are real, but they sit on the success path and are partly financeable. B's weaknesses sit on the demand path.
result.a_biggest_risk: Business owners do not release the identified retirable spend. Realization is near 25% (5-6% realized against 20% targeted in the one panel found). That leaves the fee base too thin to cover the funded engineering, and the CFO's rational alternative is to do it in-house or hire Redress at 25% once.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. They insource or buy from CareBridge instead, and plan budgets and membership are shrinking. Without that demand, the labor-bearing R3 rung that carries the revenue and margin never gets sold.

decisive_factors: Capital and control: B needs about $8-12M to reach two paid pilots and $50-80M by year 5, and the founders keep control. A needs a $340M capital stack with $130-175M of other people's equity, a proven casting operator, and a closed acquisition, so the founder is likely a deal originator with a small stake.

A's critics all rated it fatal and its structural gap is unanswered. If customers fund 60-80% of the line, they can sign a Doncasters-style deal with the plant's current owner, so the sponsor adds only the seller's liquidity. B's critics rated it serious, not fatal.

A's investor economics fail on its own numbers: about 1.8-3.3x gross, entry at a non-comp price (Precicast revenue undisclosed, sold 9/30), against GE, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters. Sources and uses also do not close. The raise, the first deal and the cycle must all go right.

Falsifiability and downside: B's two-week test costs $0-3k, and the realistic fallback is a regional or acquirable ops-services business (median about $18M, 25-30% odds of $15M or more). A has an unconditional median of $0 and about 5% odds without the operator and equity partner, and the turbine cycle may peak around 2026-2030.

A's larger upside (about $36M EBITDA, a $400M+ enterprise value) is real but low-probability and mostly accrues to the capital providers. B's ceiling is low (about $14M EBITDA at $100M revenue), but its odds per dollar and per year of founder time are better.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are mediocre, and the question is which has the better expected outcome for a capable founding team.

A has the stronger macro tailwind: turbine and aeroengine castings are short, and an acquisition buys approvals and revenue on day one. But the path to value has four gates, and each is hard.

1. The founder has to find or recruit a casting operator.
2. The team has to raise $130-175M of equity from investors who face only about 1.8-3.3x gross returns on A's own upside case.
3. The team has to win a scarce qualified asset at 2.5x revenue or less against GE/CPP, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters. The only cited comp, Precicast, has undisclosed revenue and already closed.
4. An OEM has to agree to fund a line at a non-incumbent owner. No one has found a precedent, and the customer-side value proposition is close to nil, because customers can do the same deal with the current owner.

The sponsor's edge is admitted to be non-technological. The cycle also works against it. Capacity from incumbents lands in 2028-29, and Wood Mackenzie expects orders to peak in 2026. The unconditional median is $0, and the founder probably ends up with a small stake in a capital-heavy vehicle.

B is a modest business, with a ceiling of about $14M EBITDA at $100M revenue, a thin-margin labor rung (R3), and a shrinking, cost-cutting buyer set. But it substitutes for spend plans already carry, which is a conventional outsourcing sale. It needs low initial capital and can be tested for $0-3k. Its objections (CareBridge, insourcing, savings-only pricing) were rated serious, not fatal, and the realistic fallback is an acquirable regional operations business. Odds of $15M or more are about 25-30%, which is comparable to A's odds, at a fraction of the capital and with much less founder dilution.

B wins on expected outcome per unit of capital and time.
result.a_biggest_risk: The keystone is unevidenced and probably unattainable for a new owner. No OEM has been shown to prepay or fund a line at a non-incumbent-owned caster. A first-time sponsor also cannot win a qualified asset at a sane price against GE, Pursuit, Arcline and Doncasters, and the $340M stack does not close. Customers can sign the same deal with the current owner, so the sponsor adds little.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan pays a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans insource (Centene has 338K lives in-house), buy from CareBridge, or demand savings-only terms, while their budgets and enrollment shrink. Even if they buy, R3 is a ratio-bound labor business, so the margin may not exist and revenue could stall at about $55-60M or less.

decisive_factors: Revenue quality and structure: B sells fixed PMPM, multi-year operations contracts from budget lines plans already carry, a category (outsourced Medicaid admin) buyers demonstrably accept. A sells at-will hourly labor whose conversion mechanic is self-liquidating, because every successful placement removes the billed head.

Fragility of the core economics: A's own corrected model has median EBITDA near zero or negative once free conversion after about 1,000 hours is reconciled with 25-30% attrition. It also needs a 93% staffing markup against a 35-45% norm, and the WIOA subsidy it assumed is likely ineligible. B's weak point (R3 margin asserted, demand unevidenced) is an evidence gap rather than a contradiction in its own arithmetic.

Value per revenue dollar and moat: B's $100M case is about $14M EBITDA in a recurring services-plus-tech business with scale economies and switching costs. A's is 5-8% EBITDA commodity staffing with no moat and an acquirer-takes-it ending.

Capital and time cut the other way, and this is why the call is close: A is cheaper to test and fund, at $15-30M to scale with feedback in weeks. B needs roughly $8-12M runway, 12-18 months to a first paid pilot, and $50-80M to scale.
result.reasons:
Both ideas ended round two wounded, and both have a $100M tail near 1-3% once the critics' haircuts are applied. The decision therefore rests on the middle outcomes and on which core assumption is more likely to be false.

Idea A (Level-1 Bench) has a structural problem. Its price premium is unprecedented: a 6-week trainee is billed at $52 against a $27 wage, while the only temp-technician comparable (LAUNCH) implies roughly $34-39 for experienced techs. Break-even is about $47.50, so a modest reprice kills it. The conversion terms undercut the model, because a rational shop converts early once the fee drops to zero. That roughly doubles graduates needed and takes EBITDA to about 0%. The WIOA offset is likely unavailable for hired-out staffing. At best the business becomes a thin-margin recruiter-trainer with no moat, workers' comp and liability exposure on brake and tire work, and a rational insourcing option for customers. Its two-week test is cheap, but its pass bar (non-binding order forms, no deposit) is weak.

Idea B (HCBS operations utility) has the weaker evidence base on demand. No non-Elevance plan has been shown to want it, CareBridge is entrenched, buyers are shrinking, and R3's 10-15% margin is asserted. But its objections are about unproven demand, not internal contradiction. It also sits in an established purchase category (PMPM-priced outsourced plan operations), with sticky multi-year recurring revenue, scale economics in a 24/7 desk, and a real downside outcome as a regional operations vendor with a strategic buyer set. Its cost is higher capital and a long runway to first revenue.

On expected outcome net of capital, B comes out modestly ahead, mainly on revenue quality and robustness of unit economics.
result.a_biggest_risk: Shops will not pay about a 93% staffing markup ($50+/hr on a $27 wage) for 6-week trainees instead of hiring direct at $24-28. Even if they do, free conversion after about 1,000 hours and 25-30% attrition push the unit economics to roughly zero EBITDA.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan may pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans may insource, buy from CareBridge, or demand savings-only terms, and cold-entrant sales cycles could outrun the 24-month runway while buyers are cutting budgets and exiting states.

decisive_factors: Failure mode: A degrades gracefully into a smaller but real cash-generating service group. B is binary on whether non-Elevance plans will pay a fixed fee, and there is zero demand evidence for that.

Control and agency: A needs one willing seller per deal from roughly 700 book-worthy sellers a year, and needs about 3% of them. B depends on 6-10 parents and a few dozen regional plans, each with a veto, slow sales cycles and shrinking budgets.

Capital efficiency: A has a EUR 4M first tranche backed by acquired revenue, with 40-50% of the price contingent on retention. B needs about $8-12M of seed before any proof and $50-80M for scale, against a CareBridge/Carelon incumbent acquired for about $2.7B.

Upside is higher in B ($14M EBITDA, a real exit path) but its 5-8% odds are asserted and its R3 margin is not derived. A's upside is capped by the hold-forever, no-exit structure, but its median is more likely to exist.
result.reasons:
This is a close call between two wounded ideas, and I pick A on probability of a real business, not on size of prize.

B has the bigger prize. The $101M case is roughly $14M of EBITDA with a normal exit to HHAX, Maximus or PE. A's upside is about EUR 6M EBIT, and the hold-forever steward structure caps founder liquidity. At each file's own odds, B's expected value is higher. I do not trust B's odds. Its own second-round critic puts the upside at 1-2%. Its median is conditional on a paid pilot that has no demand evidence behind it. The R3 rung, which carries about 60% of upside revenue, rests on a 10-15% margin at 95% of the buyer's in-house cost, in a ratio-bound labor business. That margin is asserted, not derived.

B is also a binary bet on a concentrated, shrinking, cost-cutting buyer set. Centene and Optum insource. Rivals already buy from CareBridge. Elevance can copy the neutrality clause in a quarter. Scale takes $50-80M.

A's central assumptions are also invented: 19% contribution, 70% retention and an unsourced B2B share. But the failure modes are operational and the team can influence them. Sellers are abundant, with 54,000 planned closures. Half the price is contingent on retention. The cheapest hub tranche is about EUR 4M. If the economics hold only at a smaller size, you still own real service revenue. That is a better floor than B's.

A still has serious problems: Brookfield-backed HomeServe can copy it, the capital is unfunded, and the invented hub economics have not been tested.

An operating partner would take the 14-day seller-ledger test and the asset-backed downside over B's pre-revenue enterprise sale into shrinking Medicaid budgets.
result.a_biggest_risk: Adverse selection on the books. Owners who cannot sell their firms hand over owner-dependent, consumer-heavy, low-margin books. Retention then falls below 70% and contribution below 15%. Hubs stay under the EUR 1.55M break-even, or never reach about EUR 3M, so the company stays a small regional group that cannot raise tranches B and C.
result.b_biggest_risk: No paying customer. Non-Elevance, non-UHC Medicaid plans insource, keep buying from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only rather than pay a fixed fee, and the scarce reachable plans are shrinking their budgets. With no demand evidence, the company dies before the $50-80M scale-up.

decisive_factors: Downside shape: A buys cash-flowing assets from sellers who demonstrably exist, so its failure mode is mostly 'no deal closes' or 'returns are mediocre'. B's failure mode is burning $10-40M of venture capital on a product with no evidence of demand, and 55-60% of its own outcomes are under $5M revenue.

Median case: A's median (about $45M revenue, about 1.5x MOIC) still returns capital. B's median ($18M revenue, roughly $2-3M EBITDA) likely fails to repay the $35M+ it needs to build R2-R3, so B's expected value rests on a 1-5% tail.

Market evidence: A has a visible stream of 2024-26 closed deals and financing. B has a negative finding (no plan asked for a non-Elevance vendor), a shrinking buyer budget, and a rival that already sells to the other plans. B's pitch drops neutrality, its original reason to exist.

Capital and time: A starts with an anchor equity check of about $10-14M, deal-by-deal and asset-backed. B needs $50-80M by year 5 with delegation approvals and 12-18 month sales cycles, and its R3 margin is asserted rather than derived.
Upside parity: A's 10% upside (about $130M revenue, about $20M EBITDA, 3.5x MOIC) is comparable to B's $100M case (about $14M EBITDA), but is several times more likely than B's 1-5%.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are wounded and neither is a good business as written, so this comes down to which objections are more likely to be fatal. A's objections attack its edge and its price. The pitch is a generic roll-up, a first-time sponsor is the least credible bidder, and strategics and PE platforms can outbid it. But a floor exists: the refined pitch's own model gives about 12.5% IRR even at 7.5x entry. The business is a real, cash-generative route-based service with a visible set of closed deals and active lenders. A can fail to close deals, but it is unlikely to blow up capital, and the 2-week owner test directly measures the one number that matters, the price sellers will accept.

B's objections attack existence of demand. No plan has asked for a vendor free of Elevance, and rivals already buy from CareBridge. Buyers are cutting administrative spend and some are exiting states. The 10-15% margin on the revenue-heavy R3 rung needs a cost advantage in a ratio-bound labor business that the pitch itself says automation cannot deliver. The $101M upside does not add up without R3, which caps it near $55-60M. Even if everything works, $100M of revenue is only about $14M of EBITDA. B's median probably does not repay the capital it needs, so nearly all its expected value sits in a 1-5% tail. A offers a similar upside tail at about 10%, a positive median, and an asset-backed floor. A is the better bet, though its median return is poor and it needs a team that does not yet exist.
result.a_biggest_risk: Sellers will not sell to a new, unproven, deal-by-deal-financed buyer at or below about 6.5x normalized EBITDA with rollover. Strategics and PE platforms with rollover set the price at 7-8x or higher and win the best targets. Anything the platform does win is adversely selected, and entry at 7.5x or above cuts the median IRR to about 4%.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Plans will insource, buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only. The buyer budget is shrinking, and the R3 margin is asserted rather than derived. Nothing found shows demand, and the $50-80M capital need makes failure expensive.

decisive_factors: Category demand is proven for B (CareBridge reached about 115k patients and sold for about $2.7B; rivals bought from it) but unproven for A, where the only documented operator customer (Kootenai) fired the operator and insourced

B's objections were rated serious, A's fatal (price, regulation, incumbents). A's rewrite fixed the legal problem only by giving up equity, leaving pass-through revenue at about 8% EBITDA, a weak moat and a cost advantage of 17-24% that the pitch never supports

Upside value and fallback: B's $101M revenue is about $14M EBITDA, and R1-R2 alone cap near $55-60M. A's $110M is mostly pass-through and sponsor-owned JV revenue, and its bear case is a $2-6M advisory boutique
B's market is larger and structural: about $1.2-1.8B of reachable spend, mandated caseload ratios and EVV data. A's market is shrinking and consolidating, with every exit going to Quest or Labcorp

A has the cheaper staged capital and a faster first-revenue product (the $25k audit), which narrows the gap. B needs $50-80M through year 5 and 12-18 months to a first paid pilot, so this is a close call
result.reasons:
Both are wounded long shots. The second-round critics put the $100M case at about 1-3% for A and 1-2% for B, and neither median holds up unconditionally. The call turns on which failure is more likely terminal and what survives if the main bet misses.

A's objections stack. Hospitals that sell want cash. The ones that stay have in-house teams, free advice from Mayo, ARUP and Chi, and national management offers. The price only works if a startup with no route density cuts the hospital's commercial cost by 17-24%, and that cost baseline is admitted to be unbenchmarked. The only observed precedent is PAML at Kootenai, where the operator was acquired by a national and the hospital left. The Medicare referral-lab rule forced a restructure into a 100% hospital-owned entity. That fix is plausible, but counsel has not confirmed it, and it removes the equity economics. What remains is a cost-plus BPO and consulting business that is hard to defend, and the bear case is a boutique.

B has real exposure too: plans are shrinking, insourcing or buying from Carelon, no plan has said it would pay a fixed fee, and R3 is a thin-margin labor business. But the category is validated by a $2.7B exit. Pain is mandated and budgeted, it avoids downstream risk licensing, and it has a larger pool. If R3 fails, R1-R2 still support a mid-sized business. Upside value is higher, and the test directly measures willingness to pay. A's lower capital and quicker audit revenue keep this close.
result.a_biggest_risk: No non-selling health system signs a 5-year open-book contract with a startup, because the price needs a cost advantage of at least 8% below the hospital's own cost (implying the operator is 17-24% cheaper) that a sub-scale entrant without route density cannot show. The alternatives are in-house, free advice from Mayo, ARUP and Chi, or a national's management offer, and even a winner risks being bought by Labcorp or Quest.
result.b_biggest_risk: Non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid plans, which are cutting costs and shrinking, will not pay a fixed non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor and instead insource, buy from CareBridge or insist on savings-only. A second risk sits behind it: the R3 coordination rung cannot earn a 10-15% margin at 95% of in-house cost, because caseload ratios stop automation from cutting headcount.

decisive_factors: A's demand is mandated and a named state or plan signs the payer line, and an acquired book produces revenue on day one. B's demand is unevidenced: no plan has been shown to pay a fixed fee to an unaffiliated vendor.

A's fatal risk is price and margin discovery (can small operators be bought at about 1x revenue with 15-20% margin). That is a binary, cheap, fast test and a known roll-up playbook with real sponsor exit buyers. B's fatal risk is a go-to-market problem: 12-30 month payer cycles, no anchor customer, shrinking buyer budgets, CareBridge and insourcing.

Median outcomes are similar and small (A about $25M revenue, B about $18M, each about $1.5-4M EBITDA), and upside tails are both poor on capital (A about 1.4-2.1x, B about $14M EBITDA at $100M). Probability of any positive outcome therefore decides, and A's is higher.

B's core differentiator (neutrality) was conceded away. What is left is a generic labor BPO priced at 95% of in-house cost with an asserted 10-15% margin, which implies an unexplained 15-20% cost advantage. A's economics are at least anchored in observable rate cards ($103-165 in choice markets).
result.reasons:
This is close, and both ideas are wounded. Neither reaches a venture-scale expected outcome, so I weighted probability of a positive result and the nature of the failure mode.

A buys real, mandated, state- or plan-signed fee streams. The thesis rests on one testable fact: whether owner-operated fiscal agents in rate-card and choice markets earn 15-20% at $103-165 PMPM and will sell around 5-6x EBITDA. That multiple is ordinary for small-business M&A. If the two-week test passes, the business is a conventional search-fund-style roll-up with cash flow from the first day and PE exits (H.I.G., General Atlantic, Alpine) already visible. If it fails, the team stops with almost nothing spent. The critic's "median is a bear case" argument applies the plan's 5-8% blended margin, which contradicts the plan's own acquisition premise. If premium margins hold, median EBITDA is nearer $3-4M.

B's objections are more likely to be fatal. There is no evidence any non-Elevance plan pays a fixed fee to a startup. Buyers are cutting costs and insourcing, CareBridge already sells to rivals, and the cold-start cycle is 12-30 months with no investor-customer anchor. The R3 margin is asserted, the neutrality pitch was dropped, and the upside arithmetic has a gap. B's capital is cheaper to stage. Its failure mode is no sale at all, and the remaining generic BPO is a low-differentiation business.

A's weakness is real: thin sector margins, liability tail, policy and fraud-crackdown exposure, and sponsor competition for targets. It is still the likelier of the two to produce a modest positive outcome.
result.a_biggest_risk: Cannot acquire a qualified small fiscal agent at a price its cash flow supports. Premium-market margins of 15-20% are unproven, sponsor-backed buyers anchor prices high, and the only cheap sellers are the money-losing ones. If so, the qualification ladder leads to statewide auctions at $68-83, where the sector loses money.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated startup. They will insource, buy from CareBridge at a discount, or insist on savings-only, while shrinking plan budgets and long procurement cycles eat the runway. The labor-heavy coordination rung then has no demonstrated margin.

decisive_factors: Unit economics: A's own critics show realistic margin of about 3-4% once an ISP alternative at 0.85-0.90x OEM sets the price, and passing the demand gate (growth of 10% or more) selects the cases where the prime loses money. B has about 34% blended gross margin and about 14% EBITDA at scale, with R1-R2 as asset-light fee work.

Capital and tail risk: A needs a $40-60M sponsor, a surety line and retained fixed-price growth risk before or at the first package, so one bad early event can end it. B's R1-R3 carry no downstream risk, a seed round of $8-12M funds two paid pilots, and the failure mode is a smaller regional business, not a blow-up.

Severity of objections: all three of A's round-1 critiques were rated fatal (copyable by Hanwha, buyers score references and bonds, insurer wrap likely uninsurable). B's were rated serious, and its core objection (will a plan pay a fixed fee?) can be answered cheaply with 12 priced-offer calls.

Market and exit: B has a larger pool ($1.2-1.8B of plan spend) and a plausible sale to HHAeXchange, Maximus, Conduent or Evolent. A's realistic median is a break-even business sold to an ISP for $20-40M, and its upside is only $4-7M EBITDA at 3% odds.
result.reasons:
Both ideas are weak and both documents say so, so this is a close call between two long shots. The question is which long shot has the better expected outcome and the less fatal objections.

A (Capped Outage) was rated fatal by all three round-1 critics. After the rewrite it is a fixed-price, bonded, date-guaranteed outage prime that owns no hardware, sells at about par to OEM and has no moat for 4-6 years. Hanwha can match the cap within 18-24 months. The economics contradict the demand test. The 12% gross margin needs a 0.77x cost basis, but a prime subcontracting shops pays about 0.85-0.90x, which leaves roughly 3-4% before bond premiums. So at $100M of revenue the profit is $4-7M EBITDA, at about 3% odds. The hard return-to-service date depends on rotor and casting slots that the ISPs hold and allocate to their own customers first. The business also holds retained fixed-price risk, needs a sponsor and a surety before event one, and realistically has first revenue in spring 2028.

B (HCBS Operations Utility) has a weak demand thesis: no evidence that neutrality sells, buyers are shrinking, and big plans insource. The rewrite responds by dropping neutrality and selling substitution of admin and coordination spend the plan already carries, priced at or below 95% of in-house cost. That is an ordinary business-process-outsourcing sale. It has higher margins, lower capital through year 5 and no risk licence until later. A bad outcome is a $5M boutique, not a loss on a bonded contract. The $100M case needs the labor-heavy R3 rung and is only about 1-8% likely, but the median of about $18M of revenue is comparable to A's, and a priced-offer call sprint can falsify it cheaply.
result.a_biggest_risk: Margin and moat collapse: against ISP alternatives at 0.85-0.90x OEM, the prime's realistic margin is about 3-4% before bonding costs, Hanwha can copy the cap, and slot allocation in a casting squeeze means it cannot deliver the hard date. The result is a thin-margin, fixed-price-risk middleman that cannot qualify for bonds or sponsor capital.
result.b_biggest_risk: No non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth plan has been shown to pay a fixed, non-contingent fee to an unaffiliated vendor, rather than insource, buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only. Even if they do, the $100M case needs the caseload-ratio-bound R3 labor rung to earn 10-15% margin at 95% of in-house cost, which is unproven.

decisive_factors: Demand evidence: B has observed willingness to pay for speed (a city paying 3.4% for years saved, 12-15% middleman premiums) and intermediaries that reached $100M+ of orders on tens of millions raised (Ayr, Giga). A has no precedent of any landlord buying a cohort carve-out, and buyer behaviour (bundling, insourcing) points the other way.

Speed and shape of the proof: B's 14-day test plus a fee-only brokering fallback gives revenue within months. A's causal proof needs a full winter trial, about 20 months, capitation revenue starts in year 3, and its core premise (top 5% of homes carry 25% or more of spend and persist) has never been measured.

Market structure: B sells into a $1.5-3B a year class with a documented multi-year shortage and real, funded buyers. A's pool is money already routed through primes' bundled contracts, and about 20% of its revenue is pass-through works at 8-12% EBITDA that must be re-competed.

Fatality of the objections: A's objections are gatekeeping (procurement turnover tests, incumbent exclusivity, Wates and Mears already selling it), which can mean zero revenue. B's objections (existing dealers, thin spread, no moat) mean a smaller dealer business rather than no business, so its downside is better.
result.reasons:
Both ideas survive only as wounded, much-reduced versions, and neither upside case ($107M or $120M of revenue) is believable. Both second-round critics put the upside at 1-3%. So the comparison comes down to which has the higher probability of becoming a profitable business of useful size, at what cost in time and capital.

B wins on that. Its pain is documented and current: 128 to 160-week lead times, buyers paying premiums, regulators pushing substation costs onto the large loads that cause them. Its competitors prove the market makes money. The refined plan concedes it is a dealer-financier with no moat. Even so, a matched-book broker and principal with a small team has a plausible path to $30M of revenue and several million dollars of gross profit. Its first test is nearly free and takes two weeks. If the premium holds, fee-only brokering can produce revenue in months.

A's premise is more novel and potentially more durable, but it is unproven at every step. The concentration data does not exist. The buyer must carve its worst homes out of bundled contracts it is simultaneously insourcing. The newco is excluded by procurement turnover and credit tests. An incumbent that already sells an adjacent product can add a gain-share schedule cheaply. Proof of causal effect takes a winter, so real revenue arrives in year 3 or later. Its capital need is lower, but its expected payoff is smaller and slower.

B's main weakness is that the shortage premium may compress as OEM capacity arrives in 2027-29, and supply access is unevidenced. That is a margin risk on a real business. A's risk is that no one buys at all.
result.a_biggest_risk: No landlord will carve its worst homes out of bundled or insourced repairs contracts for a new outcome-priced entrant. Procurement turnover and credit tests exclude a newco, primes like Wates and Mears can add a gain-share schedule cheaply, and the concentration-and-persistence premise has never been measured.
result.b_biggest_risk: Existing dealers (JCL, Maddox, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon) already deliver stocked or fast units, so the speed premium may be unavailable or collapse to a thin spread as new OEM capacity lands in 2027-29.
